newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Mobutu's defeated troops threaten camp mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu's defeated troops threaten camp mutiny.

text.p: Thousands of soldiers of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko are threatening a mutiny in a re-education camp in Democratic Republic of the Congo, government intelligence sources said on Friday.

They said complaints over conditions had raised tension in the camp at Kitona, on the west coast of the ex-Zaire. Soldiers from Mobutu's defeated army have been camped there since he was toppled by Laurent Kabila's Rwandan-backed rebel forces in May.
Kitona, at the mouth of the Congo river, was designated a training centre for the Zairean Armed Forces (FAZ) troops before potential recruitment into a new national army.
A week ago a FAZ officer was shot dead by guards when he complained of hunger and demanded food, the sources said.
The incident led to a small riot in which stones were thrown at armed guards from Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) army.
"There are reports that two ADFL soldiers were killed by the interns," one source told Reuters.
He said diarrhoea and other diseases were spreading at the camp, and that soldiers were fed little and had not been paid.
A government minister admitted the situation was of concern and said steps had been taken to address the complaints.

"The president (Kabila) himself is involved in trying to find a solution," the minister, who preferred to remain anonymous told Reuters. "Many of the officers from the former FAZ have better training than officers of the Alliance. We need them for the army."
He argued, however, that conditions for all soldiers, "even those Alliance soldiers here in Kinshasa are still far from perfect".
A senior Alliance officer said medicine and food had been sent to Kitona on Tuesday and the situation there was now calm.
"The main problem is there are so many of them. There wasn't the infrastructure," the officer said.
Neither the officer nor the intelligence sources had an estimate of the number of soldiers at the centre.

Since Kabila took power in May, renaming the country, several of Mobutu's generals have been arrested and detained, accused of corruption and mismanagement, along with other senior dignitaries from the ousted regime.
Others fled abroad along with their troops as Kabila's army marched relentlessly across the vast country.

Some former FAZ soldiers have remained at large among the civilian population, and are accused by the government of being behind a wave of robberies, murders and other violence sweeping Kinshasa and elsewhere.

However, many have submitted themselves for re-training. Some have already been re-integrated into Kabila's new rapid intervention police force which he intends to introduce to towns across the country.
The army failed to defend Mobutu's regime during Kabila's seven-month armed campaign, retreating systematically as Kabila's forces advanced.
Rarely paid under Mobutu, FAZ soldiers were renowned for making their living by extorting it from the civilian population.
Some Congo-watchers fear if Kabila does not succeed in paying the army regularly, he will face army-led anarchy similar to the final years of Mobutu's three-decade rule.
